summary: Extends LDAP so that several update operations on different entries can be grouped into one transaction. Ordinary LDAP updates are atomic only for a single entry. This is useful for things like resource provisioning. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of changing things one by one, you put several changes in a bag and the system does them all or none.

questions: how to update multiple ldap entries atomically
subtitle: Group multiple LDAP updates into a single atomic operation

tldr.problem: LDAP update operations (Add, Delete, Modify) are atomic only for a single entry. Many applications need to update multiple entries together, and partial updates create inconsistency.
tldr.mechanism: The extension introduces a Start Transaction extended operation to begin a transaction and get an identifier, a Transaction Specification control to mark updates as part of that transaction, and an End Transaction operation to commit or abort all changes as one atomic action.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now group multiple LDAP updates into a single atomic unit, solving data consistency issues in resource provisioning and other scenarios.

today: RFC 5805 is an Experimental specification. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and represents a proposed extension to LDAP for supporting multi-entry atomic updates.

sections.title: The Problem with Single-Entry Updates
sections.content: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is designed for reading and modifying directory information. When you modify an LDAP entry (such as a user account or a resource), that single modification is atomic—it either completes entirely or fails entirely. However, many real-world applications need to update multiple related entries at once. For example, when provisioning a new employee, you might need to create a user entry, add them to a group entry, update a department entry, and create a mailbox entry. If any of these operations fails partway through, you have an inconsistent directory where some entries reflect the new employee and others do not. The only workaround is to write custom application code to detect and roll back partial updates.
sections.eli5: When you change one address book entry, it either saves or doesn't. But what if you need to update ten entries together?

sections.title: How LDAP Transactions Work
sections.content: An LDAP transaction follows three steps. First, the client sends a Start Transaction Request. If the server supports transactions and allows the client, it responds with a transaction identifier. The client then sends a series of standard update requests (Add, Delete, Modify, or Rename operations), each with a Transaction Specification control attached that includes the transaction identifier. The server accepts these requests with immediate success responses but queues them internally without applying changes yet. Throughout this phase, the server remains willing and ready to receive more update operations for the same transaction. Finally, the client sends an End Transaction Request, specifying either commit or abort. If commit, the server applies all queued updates atomically in order. If abort, the server discards all queued updates. Either way, the server returns success only if all operations in the transaction either all succeeded or all failed together.
sections.eli5: You say 'start', list all the changes you want, then say 'do it all' or 'forget it'.

sections.title: Protocol Mechanisms
sections.content: The LDAP transaction extension defines four protocol elements. The Start Transaction Request uses extended operation identifier 1.3.6.1.1.21.1 with no parameters. The Start Transaction Response contains a transaction identifier if successful, or an error code if the server cannot start a transaction. The Transaction Specification Control has identifier 1.3.6.1.1.21.2 and is marked as critical. Each update operation carries this control with the transaction identifier. The control is appropriate for Add, Delete, Modify, ModifyDN (Rename), and Password Modify requests. The End Transaction Request uses extended operation identifier 1.3.6.1.1.21.3 and includes a structure with a commit flag and the transaction identifier. The End Transaction Response includes status and may provide the message ID of the operation that failed if commit failed on a particular update. An Aborted Transaction Notice is an unsolicited notification the server sends if it becomes unable to continue processing the transaction (for example, due to resource constraints), signaling the client to abandon the transaction.
sections.eli5: Each operation has a number that identifies what it is. Start is one number, end is another. The control tags updates as belonging to a transaction.

sections.title: Constraints and Interactions
sections.content: LDAP transactions have several important constraints. Transactions cannot be nested; you cannot start a transaction within a transaction. Each update request in a transaction must have a different message ID. The entire transaction must remain within a stable security context; binding to a different user or initiating a new security layer between start and end is not permitted. If the client sends a Bind or Unbind request while a transaction is outstanding, the server aborts the transaction immediately and nullifies its identifier. For distributed directories with referrals, servers may chain operations across multiple servers only if transaction semantics are guaranteed end-to-end. Clients cannot use client-side chasing of referrals within a transaction because transaction identifiers are tied to a specific LDAP connection. The Assertion control, ManageDsaIT control, and Pre/Post-Read entry controls can be used with update operations within a transaction, with responses returned through the End Transaction Response message rather than individual update responses.
sections.eli5: You can't nest transactions or switch users mid-transaction. Each change needs its own number. Distributed systems can try but must keep everything consistent.

sections.title: Applications and Benefits
sections.content: LDAP transactions enable consistent updates for resource provisioning, where a request to provision a new service requires creating or modifying multiple directory entries. A mail system might use a transaction to create a user entry, add the user to a mailing list, create a calendar entry, and assign a mailbox quota in a single atomic operation. Access control provisioning can create user entries, assign group memberships, and grant permissions all together. Application directories can maintain consistency when deploying new services that touch multiple entries. By providing atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable (ACID) properties for multi-entry updates, LDAP transactions eliminate the need for custom application-level consistency management. The server handles all-or-nothing semantics automatically.
sections.eli5: When setting up a new employee, you can create their account, add them to groups, and set permissions all at once, guaranteed to succeed or fail together.
